source.version_note: Published online 24 October 2019; Science and Engineering Ethics 26(4):2051–2068 issueAugust 2020. Both dates identify the same article, not separate publications.
source.verification_method: All 18 supplied pages read, including footnotes and full bibliography. No image-only content required rendering. Crossref verifies main work and selected bibliography identities/locators. A selected FAA system-description passage was checked for the MCAS/autopilot example; no complete accident investigation, technical certification report, legal framework or cited book was independently fully read.

citation.title: Artificial Intelligence, Responsibility Attribution, and a Relational Justification of Explainability

reading.source_scope_note: Normative philosophical argument, not an empirical study. Reconsiders control, knowledge, distributed technical/human contributions and responsibility owed to affected parties. Only-human moral agency and reason-giving are expressly bracketed assumptions, not conclusions demonstrated by a model test.
access_limits: Complete supplied article read. Cited books, original case investigations and other primary research remain secondary; there are no new participant data, effect sizes or intervention outcomes.

Crossref, related working-paper metadata and selected official FAA passages support narrow identity/factual corrections only. No current GDPR/AI-law audit or complete version comparison was performed.

study.type: Conceptual reconstruction using Aristotelian control/epistemic conditions and a relational, patient-oriented justification of explainability. No systematic review protocol, experiment, dataset, predictive model or validated governance intervention.
study.assumptions: The author explicitly sets aside whether AI could have full moral agency, freedom or awareness and assumes human responsibility for the argument. Likewise, only-human genuine explanation/reason-giving is an assumed position, not a capability benchmark or proof about all possible future AI.
study.control_and_time: Responsibility attribution spans design, data collection, deployment, operation and maintenance. Instant intervention can become impossible at system speed, but prior institutional decisions and available constraints remain relevant. Distributed contributions need not mean equal responsibility or no responsible party.
study.many_things: Interacting software, sensors, data, hardware and interfaces complicate causal reconstruction, alongside many human contributors. The author expressly cautions that a non-AI component/interface may cause a problem and that the boundary of AI is unclear. Generic automation and machine learning are not treated as technically identical.
study.epistemic_scope: Relevant knowledge includes what one is doing, moral significance, consequences, alternatives, instrument and other contributors. Merely assigning a duty does not supply knowledge or usable control. Developer/user education and organizational support are proposed, not tested.
study.relational_claim: Affected people or representatives may reasonably demand reasons from responsible agents. Technical explainability is a means supporting human/institutional answerability rather than an end in itself. Explanations should address relevant needs and context, not necessarily reconstruct every causal detail.
study.stakeholder_dialogue: Asking affected people what they need and adapting explanations to their understanding are normative proposals. They do not establish that a satisfying explanation is faithful, that every requested detail must be disclosed or that any resulting decision is justified.
study.collective_and_tragic: Distinguishes responsibility distributed among individuals from responsibility borne by a collective organization. Historical/cultural causes and tragic dilemmas may limit complete control without eliminating duties. The author calls collective responsibility contested, not a license to blame every culture member or evade repair.
study.historical_examples: Tay, early Uber collision reports and 737 MAX are illustrations, not independent investigations here. Autopilot/MCAS terminology needs correction. The 2019 GDPR characterization is a dated legal position, not current case-specific advice. No accident’s full causes or present liability are inferred.

summary: Add answerability and the problem of many things as normative/sociotechnical concepts. Enrich the many-hands entry while distinguishing legitimate distributed responsibility from psychological diffusion, and distinguish an affected person’s entitlement to reasons from perceived explainability. Correct the MCAS example and verified bibliography errors without presenting the philosophical premises as measured AI limits.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.origin: Philosophy of technology / responsibility and explanation
findings.ai_evidence_status: Normative relational responsibility concept; not an empirical finding, validated scale or proof that AI can bear human moral obligations.
findings.ai_proposal: For a consequential AI-assisted decision, identify who owes an account to whom, preserve relevant evidence and give accurate, audience-appropriate reasons with material limits visible. Enable legitimate questions, corrections and challenges. AI can support records and communication while human/institutional obligations remain explicit.
findings.novelty_rationale: A relation of owing reasons to affected parties differs from technical explanation generation, perceived clarity, mere disclosure, public blame or following an operator’s commands.
findings.evidence_scope: Printed pp 2061–2064 argue that affected parties or representatives can demand reasons and that technical systems should support that human relation. These are normative claims and proposed practices, not tests of effectiveness or machine consciousness.
findings.boundary: A convincing story is not a faithful causal account or a justification of an unjust decision. Relevant explanation need not expose private/security-sensitive detail or every causal step, but cannot hide material facts. Whether a decision is justified and what remedy is due require separate assessment; the author’s only-human premises remain assumptions.

findings.definition: Difficulty tracing causal contributions and responsibility through interacting technological components and their development histories.
findings.origin: Philosophy of technology / responsibility and explanation
findings.ai_evidence_status: Author’s explicitly proposed sociotechnical responsibility problem; no new measured psychological process or intrinsic AI defect.
findings.ai_proposal: Trace software, models, data, sensors, interfaces and maintenance across versions and organizations, then map contributions to responsible human/institutional roles. Test interactions and preserve evidence. Do not attribute a whole-system failure to AI merely because one component uses it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Technical component/interface complexity is distinct from the number of human contributors. The two problems interact, but more people and more interconnected artifacts are not the same source of attribution difficulty.
findings.evidence_scope: Printed pp 2057–2058 identify interacting artifacts, sensors, software and interfaces with long causal histories. This is broader than AI and does not itself show blame evasion or eliminate accountable duties.
findings.boundary: Complexity alone does not prove causal untraceability, a responsibility gap or nobody accountable. Technical causation, legal liability and normative duty differ; a static component list is insufficient without actual interactions and lifecycle records.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual responsibility when multiple actors contribute to an outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source directly elaborates the existing concept and adds lifecycle/interface issues captured separately by many things.
findings.evidence_scope: The normative analysis distinguishes distributed responsibility from equal shares, traces design/data/maintenance history and contrasts individual with collective-agent responsibility. No allocation formula or measured responsibility-escape effect is supplied.
findings.boundary: Legitimate shared accountability and collective institutions are not psychological diffusion. Neither technological opacity nor a collective cultural history absolves every current actor or warrants indiscriminate blame.

findings.definition: Reduced felt personal accountability when harmful conduct is treated as shared among several actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: This paper’s distributed-responsibility proposal should not be mistaken for evidence of the psychological disengagement mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The source discusses normative distribution and possible evasion, not a measured reduction in felt responsibility. Keep as a boundary-only comparison, not an additional demonstrated diffusion effect.
findings.boundary: Multiple accountable contributors can increase total accountability. Demonstrating diffusion requires unwarranted reduction in personal duty or felt responsibility, not merely naming others involved.

findings.definition: Judging that a system’s operation or recommendation is understandable and explainable.
findings.novelty_rationale: The affected party’s claim to reasons is a different kind of concept from a user’s clarity rating.

evidence.quote: what kind of explanations they need

findings.evidence_scope: The author recommends asking affected people what explanations they need and can understand. No perceived-explainability scale, comprehension test or outcome intervention is supplied; this is a normative boundary, not another measured perception effect.
findings.boundary: Reported understanding, faithful explanation and accountable reason-giving differ. Stakeholder satisfaction alone does not establish justice or truth, and a duty to explain does not require an exhaustive public disclosure of every internal detail.

source_corrections.location: Printed p 2061/PDF11 and related 737 MAX autopilot references
source_corrections.issue: The nose-down example is attributed to an advanced autopilot system.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: For the MCAS behavior at issue, the FAA describes the original system as operating in manual flight with autopilot off and flaps retracted. MCAS flight-control augmentation and autopilot are different. This narrow correction does not determine the complete accident causal chain or responsibility.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Official FAA Review Section 6 system-description excerpt retrieved/read; full report, accident records and all design revisions were not read or audited.

source_corrections.verification_scope: Metadata only; original full article not independently read.

source_corrections.location: Printed p 2067, Kleinberg et al. reference
source_corrections.issue: Mullainathany is misspelled and journal pagination is 1–62.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The author is Sendhil Mullainathan. The final Journal of Legal Analysis article is 10:113–174,DOI10.1093/jla/laz 001. Crossref lists issue 2018 and online 22 April 2019; the source’s 2019 date is not simply rejected.

methodological_limits: Conceptual validity and normative persuasion are not empirical validation. The paper supplies no prevalence, psychological effect size, safety test or proof of proposed safeguards.
Technical transparency, source-code access, explanation, human comprehension, justified reasons and an effective remedy differ; none automatically establishes the others.

A complex machine-learning system may be partly explainable and a large symbolic system hard to comprehend. The historical symbolic-versus-black-box contrast is not imported as an absolute architecture law.
Human accountability should not be inferred as unlimited sole blame for the nearest operator. Control, knowledge, feasible alternatives and upstream lifecycle roles require case-specific evidence.
The paper explicitly brackets legal analysis and machine moral agency. Its philosophical and 2019 regulatory assumptions must not be stated as universally settled current facts.
Early media examples and secondary quoted studies are not independently verified accident findings or complete readings of original sources.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Both connect usable control/knowledge with human accountability, but this source centers the affected party’s demand for reasons. Professional authority alone does not settle patient rights, and a normative framework is not a tested clinical intervention.
A framework predicting public responsibility judgments differs from a normative account of owed reasons. Causal contribution, perceived blame and justified accountability remain separate.

Perceived explainability in a self-report scale differs from answerability to affected people. A positive or negative attitude association neither establishes nor defeats the normative obligation to give relevant, accurate reasons.

deferred.reason: Important practices and roles within the answerability account. Retain them in that entry rather than add loosely separable labels without a distinct operational account here.

The author explicitly distinguishes distributed individual duties from collective-agent responsibility and treats the latter as contested. Preserve the distinction in existing many-hands notes before adding a broad potentially overlapping framework row.
Brief philosophical lead, not an independent demonstrated behavioral mechanism or proof that a particular AI dilemma is insoluble. Consult the cited original works.

deferred.term: Current right to explanation under GDPR
deferred.reason: The paper’s 2019 characterization is historical. No present legal conclusion follows without checking the applicable provisions, case law and specific decision.

limitations: All cited books, including Aristotle, Levinas, responsibility monographs and robot-ethics books, remain secondary. One article has one source identity regardless of online/issue dates. No new bibliometric total or automatic ethical/harm edges are added.
